title: Abelian torsors and derived first cohomology on any small site
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a site small relative to the sheaf universe [def-weil-size-convention, def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology], and let $G$ be an abelian sheaf. Put $\Gamma(\mathcal C,F)=\operatorname{Hom}(*,F)$ for the final sheaf $*$, and $H^q(\mathcal C,G)=R^q\Gamma(\mathcal C,-)(G)$, computed using injective resolutions [def-sp-injective-resolutions]. A $G$-torsor is a sheaf of sets $T$ with a $G$-action, with $T\to *$ locally surjective, such that $(g,t)\mapsto(g+t,t)$ is an isomorphism $G\times T\to T\times T$. Let $\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}$ be the sheafification of the constant integer presheaf, and $\mathbf Z[T]$ the sheafification of $U\mapsto\mathbf Z[T(U)]$, where the latter denotes the free abelian group. Define $E_T$ as the quotient abelian sheaf of $G\oplus\mathbf Z[T]$ by the subsheaf generated locally by $(g,[t]-[g+t])$. There is a short exact sequence $0\to G\to E_T\xrightarrow{p_T}\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}\to0$, where $p_T([t])=1$, and $t\mapsto[t]$ identifies $T$ equivariantly with the sheaf fibre $p_T^{-1}(1)$. The rule $\kappa_G([T])=\delta_{E_T}(1)$ is a canonical bijection from isomorphism classes of $G$-torsors to $H^1(\mathcal C,G)$. More generally, for every short exact sequence $0\to G\to E\xrightarrow p\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}\to0$, its fibre $p^{-1}(1)$ is a $G$-torsor and $\kappa_G([p^{-1}(1)])=\delta_E(1)$. Here $\delta_E$ is the connecting homomorphism of the derived global-section long exact sequence. The bijection carries the trivial torsor $G$ to zero and the contracted product $(T\times T')/G$ (the sheafification of the sectionwise quotient by $(t,t')\mapsto(g+t,t'-g)$) to addition in $H^1$. No final object of $\mathcal C$ is assumed.

proof.text: Global sections are compatible families of sections over all objects, so they form an abelian group. They preserve kernels: a compatible family killed by a morphism is uniquely a compatible family in its sectionwise kernel. They preserve finite biproducts by taking the two components. Thus $\Gamma$ is additive and left exact, with no final site object needed. The category of abelian sheaves has enough injectives. Apply the right-derived universal delta-functor theorem and its degree-zero identification to $\Gamma$: every short exact sequence has the natural, additive connecting maps in the statement. In particular, for $0\to G\xrightarrow{i}I\xrightarrow{r}Q\to0$ with $I$ injective, $H^1(I)=0$: the resolution $I\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}I\to0\to\cdots$ computes it as zero. Hence $\delta_I:\Gamma(Q)\to H^1(G)$ is surjective and has kernel $r\Gamma(I)$.

proof.text:
Form the quotient $E_T$ specified in the statement; quotients are sheafifications of presheaf quotients because sheafification is a left adjoint. Its relations give $[g+t]=g+[t]$, so $j(g)$ is represented by $(g,0)$ and the augmentation $p_T$ is well defined. On any object with a chosen $t_0\in T(U)$, write $t=d(t,t_0)+t_0$. Over every object mapping to $U$ the mutually inverse coordinate formulas are
$$ (a,\sum n_t[t])\longmapsto(a+\sum n_t d(t,t_0),\sum n_t),\qquad (a,n)\longmapsto j(a)+n[t_0]. $$
The first kills each relation, and the second followed by the first is the identity; the other composite is the identity by $[t]=j(d(t,t_0))+[t_0]$. These natural formulas extend across sheafification. They identify $E_T$ locally with $G\oplus\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}$, $j$ with the first inclusion and $p_T$ with the second projection. Indeed every section of a sheafified quotient and every equality in it is represented after a cover, and exact sheafification preserves the kernels and quotients used here. The torsor supplies such local $t_0$ over every object. Thus $j$ is injective, its image is $\ker p_T$, and $p_T$ is locally surjective, hence epic. In these coordinates $[t]$ is $(d(t,t_0),1)$, so $T\to p_T^{-1}(1)$ is equivariant and locally bijective, hence an isomorphism. This proves the asserted short exact sequence and fibre formula.

proof.text: For any short exact sequence $0\to G\xrightarrow{j}E\xrightarrow p\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}\to0$, let $P=p^{-1}(1)$. The epimorphism $p$ lifts $1$ locally, and sectionwise exactness at $E$ says that two lifts differ by a unique $j(g)$. Thus $P$ is a torsor. Define $v:E_P\to E$ by $v(g)=j(g)$ and $v([e])=e$ for $e\in P$. This respects $[g+e]=g+[e]$ and commutes with the inclusion of $G$ and projection to $\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}$. Locally choose $e_0\in P(U)$; then both extensions have coordinates $(g,n)\mapsto j(g)+ne_0$ and $v$ is the identity in these coordinates. Consequently $v$ is an isomorphism. A torsor isomorphism $T\to T'$ likewise induces an extension isomorphism by $g\mapsto g$, $[t]\mapsto[\varphi(t)]$. Naturality of connecting homomorphisms now shows that $\kappa_G([T])=\delta_{E_T}(1)$ is well defined on torsor isomorphism classes, and that $\kappa_G([P])=\delta_E(1)$ for every extension in the statement.

proof.text: Fix one embedding $i:G\hookrightarrow I$ with $I$ injective and put $Q=I/G$. For $q\in\Gamma(Q)$ let $L_q$ be the sheaf of lifts of $q$ to $I$, with translation through $i$. It is a torsor: local surjectivity of $I\to Q$ gives local lifts and its sectionwise kernel is $G$. The rule $g\mapsto i(g)$, $[x]\mapsto x$ gives $E_{L_q}\to I$. Together with the identity on $G$ and the map $\mathbf Z_{\mathcal C}\to Q$ sending $1$ to the compatible family $q$, it is a morphism from the canonical extension of $L_q$ to $0\to G\to I\to Q\to0$. Naturality gives $\kappa_G([L_q])=\delta_I(q)$. Since $\delta_I$ is surjective by step 1, every cohomology class is in the image of $\kappa_G$.

source.place: Tag 03AJ (lemma-torsors-h1), lifting-fibre inverse and the first inverse identity

proof.text: For a torsor $T$, injectivity of $I$ extends $i:G\to I$ across the monomorphism $j:G\to E_T$ to a homomorphism $b:E_T\to I$, with $bj=i$. The images $r(b([t]))$ do not depend on the local choice of $t$: replacing $t$ by $g+t$ adds $i(g)$, which $r$ kills. Choose local torsor sections on a covering of each object. Their images agree on overlaps because two torsor sections differ uniquely by $g$, so the sheaf axiom glues them to $q_U\in Q(U)$. Uniqueness makes all $q_U$ compatible with every restriction, hence gives $q\in\Gamma(Q)$. The map $t\mapsto b([t])$ identifies $T$ with $L_q$: it is equivariant and is a bijection wherever a section $t_0$ exists, because $g+t_0$ maps to $i(g)+b([t_0])$ and these are precisely the lifts of $q$. Thus it is an isomorphism of sheaves. This proves the other inverse assertion used in the source, rather than assuming it.

source.place: Tag 03AJ (lemma-torsors-h1), omitted mutual-inverse verification, supplied using its injective-quotient construction

proof.text: If $\kappa_G([T])=\kappa_G([T'])$, step 5 identifies $T$ and $T'$ with $L_q$ and $L_{q'}$ for the same chosen $I$. Step 4 and the exact sequence in step 1 imply $q'-q=r(a)$ for a global section $a\in\Gamma(I)$. Translation $x\mapsto x+a$ is a restriction-compatible $G$-equivariant isomorphism $L_q\to L_{q'}$, with inverse $x\mapsto x-a$. Therefore $T\cong T'$, proving injectivity. The construction of $E_T$ and its boundary involved no $I$, so this proves a canonical bijection; the auxiliary choice of $I$ was used only to prove its bijectivity.

proof.text: For the trivial torsor $G$, $[0]\in\Gamma(E_G)$ maps to $1$. Exactness of the global-section long exact sequence gives $\delta_{E_G}(1)=0$.

proof.text:
Let $S=(T\times T')/G$ with the antidiagonal action in the statement. The residual action is $a\cdot[t,t']=[a+t,t']=[t,a+t']$. Locally choose $t_0,t'_0$. If $t=g+t_0$ and $t'=h+t'_0$, the orbit has the unique representative $[ (g+h)+t_0,t'_0]$. Thus the sectionwise quotient is locally $G$, the residual action is translation, and sheafification gives a $G$-torsor $S$. Choose extensions $b:E_T\to I$ and $b':E_{T'}\to I$ of the same $i:G\to I$ as in step 5, giving global sections $q,q'$ of $Q$. The map $(t,t')\mapsto b([t])+b'([t'])$ is invariant under $(t,t')\mapsto(g+t,t'-g)$, since the two changes are $i(g)$ and $-i(g)$. It therefore factors through the sectionwise quotient and uniquely through its sheafification $S$, by the sheafification universal property. Its image in $Q$ is $q+q'$, and it is $G$-equivariant. On the above local coordinates it bijects $S$ with $L_{q+q'}$, so it is a torsor isomorphism. By step 4 and additivity of the connecting map,
$$\kappa_G([S])=\delta_I(q+q')=\delta_I(q)+\delta_I(q')=\kappa_G([T])+\kappa_G([T']).$$
This also checks the sign of the contracted-product action.
